text: A playable NYC subway performance game
A local 3D game with an optional real-time visual enhancement layer
A performance game inside a moving NYC subway car
The player is a street performer working a crowded car. Every move earns attention, but every mistake costs safety.
The prototype keeps play readable first: the car, the crowd, and the rules stay visible during performance.
The target moved from flat action to a physical space
Strong game loop, limited spatial depth
Enclosed train, solid obstacles, articulated riders
The visual ambition grew from a playable canvas into a contained 3D world with readable physical rules.
The project grew through short, testable passes
Each pass answered one practical question before the next layer was added.
The working rule was simple: keep the game playable without Reactor, then add visual ambition around a stable simulation.
The game loop turns attention into movement
The player constantly chooses between performance and safe positioning.
Tips are the visible reward. Strikes, noise, balance, and clearance create the pressure underneath.
The train is a playable object, not a backdrop
The renderer uses a 1280 × 832 gameplay target while the browser scales the canvas and interface to the viewport.

text: Characters begin as roles, then become riders
MESHY AI → GLB → RIGGED RUNTIME ACTOR
Seated, standing, commuter, and role-specific riders
Meshy supplies the base humanoid rigs. The game adds procedural poses for contact, rests, flips, falls, and pole work.
The source GLBs remain intact; runtime copies use stable web-safe names and shared loading code.
Movement is built around contact and consequence
A train lurch is a test of preparation.
Q beside a reachable rod → brace
Clearance is checked through the stunt
The simulation owns the timing, collision, balance, score, and strike. Rendering follows the result.
The visual goal is fast action that still reads clearly: hands, poles, bodies, and consequences remain legible.
The interface came from Figma, then became live state
SVG surfaces and the Koulen display type were brought into the browser as editable HTML/CSS, while values stay connected to the simulation.
The Figma file defines the visual language; the game state defines what the UI is allowed to say.
A simple architecture keeps the experiment changeable
One state object drives the rules. Rendering stays downstream.
The same simulation can render locally, record to MP4, or feed the optional visual model.
The separation makes the offline game dependable and keeps Reactor from owning the player’s physics.
Reactor adds a visual pass after the game is already working

Consistent stainless-steel NYC subway car, curved orange benches, dark speckled floor, side fluorescent lights, dim aisle, worn ads, grime, fingerprints, graffiti, tunnel motion. Preserve framing, poles, players, passengers, and gameplay actions.
Wired in the local app. Stable LIVE verification remains the next technical gate.
Reactor can repaint the frames. It should not decide whether a player collides, grips, falls, scores, or wins.
The prototype is documented as a playable system
Evidence includes gameplay videos, contact sheets, browser captures, character loading checks, and automated regression tests.
The next milestone is visual consistency under pressure
Responsive layout, character loading, camera framing, fast actions
Verify Reactor in a controlled scene
Token, SDK, source publishing, prompt acceptance, returned video
One subway interior image before a session begins
Pole grip, flips, turbulence falls, dense crowds
Clean walkthrough, source, documentation, and MP4 evidence
The exhibition version should show a reliable local game first, then make the Reactor pass visible as an enhancement rather than a dependency.
An exhibition-ready prototype about movement, attention, and shared space.

BUILD THE WORLD FIRST.
THEN LET THE VISUAL LAYER PUSH IT FURTHER.
